title: Remembering without hatred
hookLine: the Ardas names martyrs, not enemies; memory is for courage, not revenge

lines: AND NOT ONE ENEMY IS NAMED.
cards: Partway through the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings, comes a passage that's hard to hear.

It remembers Sikhs cut limb from limb, scalped, broken on the wheel, sawn apart, who gave their heads and kept their faith. The congregation stands with folded hands and answers Waheguru. And something is missing.
The governors, the generals, the invaders who did these things: their names aren't there. Today: remembering without hatred.

teach.h: THE PRAYER NAMES THOSE WHO STOOD.
teach.b: Start with what the prayer keeps. The Ardas names the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Piare, and then the ones whose names are lost, by what they endured and what they held on to: their hair, their faith, their Guru.
Memory pointed at the ones who stood, not the ones who struck.

teach.h: NO ONE IS MY ENEMY, NO ONE A STRANGER.
teach.b: Second, a line Guru Arjan left in the Guru Granth Sahib, here in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone.

It comes from a Guru who was himself put to death, and it can be heard alongside the long list of martyrs. It doesn't say nothing bad happened. It says the heart doesn't have to be organized around the people who did it.

teach.h: IT ENDS ASKING THE GOOD OF ALL.
teach.b: Third, how the prayer ends. After all that suffering, the Ardas asks for sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Everyone, not everyone except them.
A few weeks back, this path met a minister whose grief turned into a slaughter; Sikhs tell that story too.
Read this way, the Ardas keeps grief from being handed on as hatred. When Sikhs stand and remember, the prayer doesn't ask who to pay back. It asks, in effect, could I stand like that?

how: Sikhs stand for the Ardas at the close of services and daily prayers; one passage remembers the martyrs by what they endured, the congregation answers Waheguru, and the prayer closes asking for the good of all.

o: a hymn of the Gurus sung at dawn in the gurdwara
the reading that opens the Guru Granth Sahib
the standing prayer that closes Sikh gatherings

games.q: what the prayer keeps — tap the pairs.

s: the Ardas lists the names of the persecutors so they are never forgotten
it names the martyrs and what they endured. the enemies aren't named.
the Ardas ends asking for the good of all
sarbat da bhala: the well-being of everyone.
remembering the martyrs means not talking about what happened
the passage is plain about the suffering. it just points memory at the ones who stood.

games.q: you're putting together the words a whole community will pray, standing, every day. you have to remember people who were tortured to death. what do you put in?
o: the names of the men who did it, so nobody forgets.
what the martyrs endured and kept, and a closing wish for everyone's good.
nothing at all, it's too painful.
games.why: the Ardas does the second: it remembers the martyrs by what they endured, names no enemy, and closes with sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

practice: Bring to mind someone who went through something hard, in your family or your own life, and see it plainly. If your attention drifts to the one who caused it, bring it gently back to the one who endured: what did they hold on to?
If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out; if not, let any anger pass like weather.

wordCard.voice: Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings. It names the martyrs by what they endured, names no enemy, and ends asking the good of all. Today's word.
